translations.literal: Only you, sir, are a founding minister of the state; Song and Heng send down blessing; you hold the upper lands of the Nine Provinces and bear the great talent of an age—fit this moment and seek your own blessing.
translations.idiomatic: You alone are the state's founding pillar; fortune falls on you from the sacred peaks; you hold the heartland of the realm and bear the talent of the age—seize this moment and secure your own blessing.

sentences.zh: 所承良訊，非仆深心，天下其謂我何，有國非吾節也。

translations.literal: The fine message you offer is not my inmost heart; what would the world say of me? To hold a realm is not my principle.
translations.idiomatic: Your generous proposal is not my true mind; what would the world say of me? To take a kingdom is not my way.

sentences.zh: 淒淒孤懇，此不盡陳。

translations.literal: My solitary plea is sorrowful; this cannot fully be told.
translations.idiomatic: My lonely plea is full of grief; I cannot say all of it.

sentences.zh: 五月，梁祖遣其將康懷英率兵十萬圍潞州，懷英驅率士眾，築壘環城，城中音信斷絕。

translations.literal: Fifth month, the Liang Founder sent his general Kang Huaiying with a hundred thousand troops to besiege Lu Prefecture; Huaiying drove the soldiers, built stockades ringing the city, and word within the walls was cut off.
translations.idiomatic: In the fifth month the Liang Founder sent Kang Huaiying with a hundred thousand men to besiege Lu; Huaiying drove his troops to ring the city with camps and cut off all news from within.

sentences.zh: 武皇遣周德威將兵赴援，德威軍於餘吾，率先鋒挑戰，日有俘獲，懷英不敢即戰。

translations.literal: Wuhuang sent Zhou Dewei with troops to relieve the city; Dewei camped at Yuyu, led the vanguard to challenge daily, and took captives each day; Huaiying dared not give battle at once.
translations.idiomatic: Wuhuang sent Zhou Dewei to relieve the city; Dewei camped at Yuyu, led the van in daily skirmishes, and took prisoners every day; Huaiying would not fight a pitched battle.

sentences.zh: 梁祖以懷英無功，乃以李思安代之。

translations.literal: The Liang Founder, because Huaiying had no success, replaced him with Li Si'an.
translations.idiomatic: Because Huaiying had achieved nothing, the Liang Founder replaced him with Li Si'an.

sentences.zh: 思安引軍將營於潞城，周德威以五千騎搏之，梁軍大敗，斬首千餘級。

translations.literal: Si'an led troops to camp at Lucheng; Zhou Dewei with five thousand cavalry engaged them; the Liang army was greatly defeated and more than a thousand heads were taken.
translations.idiomatic: Si'an moved to camp at Lucheng; Zhou Dewei struck with five thousand horse, routed the Liang army, and took more than a thousand heads.

sentences.zh: 思安退保堅壁，別築外壘，謂之「夾塞」，以抗我之援軍。

translations.literal: Si'an withdrew to hold a strong wall and separately built outer stockades called the "twin forts" to block our relief army.
translations.idiomatic: Si'an fell back behind stout walls and built outer camps called the "Twin Forts" to block our relief.

sentences.zh: 梁祖調發山東之民以供饋運，德威日以輕騎掩之，運路艱阻，眾心益恐。

translations.literal: The Liang Founder mobilized the people of Shandong for supply transport; Dewei daily sent light cavalry to harry them; the supply routes grew hard and hearts grew more fearful.
translations.idiomatic: The Liang Founder drafted the people of Shandong for convoys; Dewei sent light horse against them daily; the routes grew perilous and morale sank.

sentences.zh: 李思安乃自東南山口築夾道，連接夾寨，以通饋運，自是梁軍堅保夾塞。

translations.literal: Li Si'an then built a walled road from the southeastern mountain pass linking the twin forts to open supply transport; from then on the Liang army held the twin forts firmly.
translations.idiomatic: Li Si'an then built a walled road from the southeast pass to link the twin forts and keep supplies moving; after that the Liang army held the forts in strength.

sentences.zh: 冬十月，武皇有疾，是時晉陽城無故自壞，占者惡之。

translations.literal: Tenth month of winter, Wuhuang fell ill; at that time the walls of Jinyang collapsed without cause, and diviners took it as ill omen.
translations.idiomatic: In the tenth month of winter Wuhuang fell ill; the walls of Jinyang collapsed for no reason, and diviners called it a bad sign.

sentences.zh: 天祐五年正月戊子朔，武皇疾革。

translations.literal: On the wuzi new moon of the first month of Tianyou 5, Wuhuang's illness turned critical.
translations.idiomatic: On the new moon of the first month of Tianyou 5 Wuhuang grew deathly ill.

sentences.zh: 辛卯，崩於晉陽，年五十三。

translations.literal: On xinmao he died at Jinyang, aged fifty-three.
translations.idiomatic: On xinmao he died at Jinyang, aged fifty-three.

sentences.zh: 遣令薄葬，發喪後二十七日除服。

translations.literal: His testament ordered a plain burial and mourning dress laid aside twenty-seven days after the funeral.
translations.idiomatic: He ordered a plain burial and that mourning dress end twenty-seven days after the funeral.

sentences.zh: 莊宗即位，追諡武皇帝，廟號太祖，陵在雁門。

translations.literal: When Zhuangzong took the throne he posthumously titled him Martial Emperor, temple name Taizu, tomb at Yanmen.
translations.idiomatic: Zhuangzong posthumously named him Martial Emperor, gave him the temple name Taizu, and buried him at Yanmen.

sentences.zh: 《五代史補》：太祖武皇，本朱耶赤心之後，沙陁部人也。

translations.literal: The 《Supplement to the History of the Five Dynasties》 says: Taizu Wuhuang was originally of the Zhuoye Chixin line, a man of the Shatuo tribe.
translations.idiomatic: The 《Supplement to the History of the Five Dynasties》 says Wuhuang Taizu was descended from Zhuoye Chixin and was of the Shatuo tribe.

sentences.zh: 其先生於雕窠中，酋長以其異生，諸族傳養之，遂以「諸爺」為氏，言非一父所養也。

translations.literal: His ancestor was born in an eagle's nest; the chieftain, because the birth was strange, had the clans raise him in turn, and they took "Zhu Ye" as the clan name, meaning not raised by one father.
translations.idiomatic: An ancestor was born in an eagle's nest; the chieftain, seeing the omen, had the clans rear him by turns, and they took "Zhu Ye" as the clan name—"not one father's child."

sentences.zh: 其後言訛，以「諸」為「朱」，以 「爺」為「耶」。

translations.literal: Later the words shifted: "Zhu" was written as the Zhu 朱 character, and "Ye" as the Ye 耶 character.
translations.idiomatic: Later the name was corrupted: "Zhu-ye" became the Zhu and Ye of his surname.

sentences.zh: 至太祖生，眇一目，長而驍勇，善騎射，所向無敵，時謂之「獨眼龍」，大為部落所疾。

translations.literal: When Taizu was born he had one blind eye; grown he was fierce and brave, skilled in horse and bow, unmatched wherever he went; men called him the "One-Eyed Dragon," and the tribes greatly resented him.
translations.idiomatic: Taizu was born with one blind eye; grown he was fierce, a master of horse and bow, unbeaten in battle, and men called him the "One-Eyed Dragon"—much hated in the tribe.

sentences.zh: 太祖恐禍及，遂舉族歸唐，授雲州刺史，賜姓李，名克用。

translations.literal: Taizu feared disaster would reach him, led his whole clan to submit to Tang, was made prefect of Yunzhou, granted the surname Li, and named Keyong.
translations.idiomatic: Fearing harm, he led his clan to Tang, was made prefect of Yun, given the surname Li, and named Keyong.

sentences.zh: 黃巢犯長安，自北引兵赴難，功成，遂拜太原節度使，封晉王。

translations.literal: When Huang Chao struck Chang'an he led troops south from the north to the rescue; when the work succeeded he was made military commissioner of Taiyuan and enfeoffed Prince of Jin.
translations.idiomatic: When Huang Chao took Chang'an he marched from the north to save the throne; for his service he became military commissioner of Taiyuan and Prince of Jin.

sentences.zh: 武皇之有河東也，威聲大振。

translations.literal: When Wuhuang held Hedong his martial renown greatly rose.
translations.idiomatic: Once Wuhuang held Hedong his fame as a warrior soared.

sentences.zh: 淮南楊行密常恨識其狀貌，因使畫工詐為商賈，往河東寫之。

translations.literal: Huainan's Yang Xingmi often regretted not knowing his appearance, and therefore sent a painter disguised as a merchant to Hedong to paint him.
translations.idiomatic: Yang Xingmi of Huainan, who had never seen his face, sent a painter disguised as a merchant to Hedong to capture his likeness.

sentences.zh: 畫工到，未幾，人有知其謀者，擒之。

translations.literal: When the painter arrived, before long someone knew the plot and seized him.
translations.idiomatic: The painter had barely arrived when someone uncovered the plot and seized him.

sentences.zh: 武皇初甚怒，既而謂所親曰：「且吾素眇一目，試召之使寫，觀其所為如何。

translations.literal: Wuhuang at first was very angry, then said to those close to him: "I have long had one blind eye—summon him to paint and see what he does.
translations.idiomatic: Wuhuang was furious at first, then told his intimates, "I have been blind in one eye for years—bring him in and see what he paints.

sentences.zh: 」及至，武皇按膝厲聲曰：「淮南使汝來寫吾真，必畫工之尤也，寫吾不及十分，即價下便是死汝之所矣。

translations.literal: 」When he came, Wuhuang pressed his knee and said in a harsh voice: "Huainan sent you to paint my likeness—you must be a master painter. Paint me less than perfect and the lowered price is where you die."
translations.idiomatic: 」When the man came, Wuhuang struck his knee and thundered, "Huainan sent you to paint me—you must be their best. Fall short by a tenth and that lowered price is your death."

sentences.zh: 」畫工再拜下筆。

translations.literal: 」The painter bowed again and set brush to silk.
translations.idiomatic: 」The painter bowed again and began to paint.

sentences.zh: 時方盛暑，武皇執八角扇，因寫扇角半遮其面。

translations.literal: It was the height of summer; Wuhuang held an eight-cornered fan, and the painter therefore painted the fan corner half hiding his face.
translations.idiomatic: It was midsummer; Wuhuang held an eight-sided fan, and the painter hid half his face behind the fan in the picture.

sentences.zh: 武皇曰：「汝諂吾也。

translations.literal: Wuhuang said: "You flatter me."
translations.idiomatic: Wuhuang said, "You flatter me."

sentences.zh: 」遽使別寫之，又應聲下筆，畫其臂弓撚箭之狀，仍微合一目以觀箭之曲直，武皇大喜，因厚賂金帛遣之。

translations.literal: 」He at once had another painting made; again the brush answered at once, painting him with bow on arm twisting an arrow, still slightly closing one eye to judge the arrow's curve; Wuhuang was greatly pleased and gave gold and silk in rich reward before sending him away.
translations.idiomatic: 」He ordered another portrait; the painter worked at once, showing him with bow on arm and arrow drawn, one eye narrowed to sight the shaft; Wuhuang was delighted, gave him gold and silk, and sent him away.

sentences.zh: 《五代史闕文》：世傳武皇臨薨，以三矢付莊宗曰：「一矢討劉仁恭，汝不先下幽州，河南未可圖也。

translations.literal: The 《Lost Chapters of the History of the Five Dynasties》 says: Tradition holds that as Wuhuang lay dying he gave Zhuangzong three arrows, saying: "One arrow to punish Liu Rengong—you cannot take Henan until you first take Youzhou.
translations.idiomatic: The 《Lost Chapters of the History of the Five Dynasties》 says: Tradition holds that on his deathbed Wuhuang gave Zhuangzong three arrows, saying, "One to punish Liu Rengong—you must take Youzhou before you can dream of Henan.

sentences.zh: 一矢擊契丹，且曰阿保機與吾把臂而盟，結為兄弟，誓復唐家社稷，今背約附賊，汝必伐之。

translations.literal: One arrow to strike the Khitan—and he said Abaoji clasped arms with me and swore brotherhood, vowing to restore the Tang realm; now he breaks the pact and joins the bandit—you must attack him.
translations.idiomatic: One to strike the Khitan—Abaoji swore brotherhood with me and vowed to restore Tang; now he breaks faith and joins the traitor—you must attack him.

sentences.zh: 一矢滅朱溫，汝能成吾誌，死無憾矣！

translations.literal: One arrow to destroy Zhu Wen—if you can fulfill my will I die without regret!"
translations.idiomatic: One to destroy Zhu Wen—if you fulfill my will I die content!"

sentences.zh: 」莊宗藏三矢於武皇廟庭。

translations.literal: 」Zhuangzong stored the three arrows in the court of Wuhuang's temple.
translations.idiomatic: 」Zhuangzong kept the three arrows in Wuhuang's temple court.

sentences.zh: 及討劉仁恭，命幕吏以少牢告廟，請一矢，盛以錦囊，使親將負之以為前驅。

translations.literal: When he campaigned against Liu Rengong he ordered a staff officer to report to the temple with a young victim, took one arrow, placed it in a brocade bag, and had a trusted general carry it before the van.
translations.idiomatic: When he marched on Liu Rengong he had a clerk offer sacrifice at the temple, took one arrow in a brocade bag, and had a trusted general carry it before the van.

sentences.zh: 凱旋之日，隨俘馘納矢於太廟。

translations.literal: On the day of triumph he presented the arrow with the captives and spoils at the Grand Temple.
translations.idiomatic: On the day of victory he brought the arrow back with prisoners and spoils to the Grand Temple.

sentences.zh: 伐契丹，滅朱氏亦如之。

translations.literal: Against the Khitan and in destroying the Zhu clan he did the same.
translations.idiomatic: He did the same against the Khitan and in destroying the Zhu house.

sentences.zh: 又，武皇眇一目，謂之「獨眼龍。

translations.literal: Further, Wuhuang had one blind eye and was called the "One-Eyed Dragon.
translations.idiomatic: It adds that Wuhuang had one blind eye and was called the "One-Eyed Dragon.

sentences.zh: 」性喜殺，左右有小過失，必置於死。

translations.literal: 」He delighted in killing; attendants who made small faults were always put to death.
translations.idiomatic: 」He loved killing; a small slip by an attendant meant death.

sentences.zh: 初諱眇，人無敢犯者，嘗令寫真，畫工即為撚箭之狀，微瞑一目，圖成而進，武皇大悅，賜予甚厚。）

translations.literal: At first his blind eye was taboo and none dared mention it; once he ordered his portrait painted, and the painter at once showed him twisting an arrow, one eye slightly closed; when the picture was done and presented Wuhuang was greatly pleased and gave a rich reward.)
translations.idiomatic: His blind eye was once taboo; when he ordered a portrait the painter showed him drawing a bow with one eye narrowed; Wuhuang was delighted and rewarded him richly.)

sentences.zh: 史臣曰：武皇肇跡陰山，赴難唐室，逐豺狼於魏闕，殄氛祲於秦川，賜姓受封，奄有汾、晉，可謂有功矣。

translations.literal: The historian says: Wuhuang began his track at Yinshan, rushed to aid the Tang house, drove wolves from the Wei gate, and extinguished evil vapors in Qinchuan; he received surname and fief and held Fen and Jin—this may be called merit.
translations.idiomatic: The historian writes: Wuhuang rose from Yinshan, saved the Tang court, drove wolves from the capital, and cleared rebellion from Qinchuan; he took a surname, a fief, and held Fen and Jin—this was merit.

sentences.zh: 然雖茂勤王之績，而非無震主之威。

translations.literal: Yet though his service to the throne was abundant, he was not without awe that shook the ruler.
translations.idiomatic: Yet for all his zeal in the king's service, he also inspired fear in his lord.

sentences.zh: 及朱旗屯渭曲之師，俾翠輦有石門之幸，比夫桓、文之輔周室，無乃有所愧乎！

translations.literal: When Zhu banners camped at Weiqu and the green carriage knew the fortune of Shimen, compared with Huan and Wen aiding the Zhou house, was he not somewhat shamed!
translations.idiomatic: When Zhu armies camped on the Wei bend and the imperial carriage met Shimen's fate, beside Huan and Wen who upheld Zhou, he had reason to blush.

sentences.zh: 洎失援於蒲、絳，久垂翅於並、汾，若非嗣子之英才，豈有興王之茂業。

translations.literal: By the time he lost aid at Pu and Jiang and long hung his wings at Bing and Fen, had his heir not been a man of talent, how could there have been a founding king's great work.
translations.idiomatic: When he lost Pu and Jiang and languished at Bing and Fen, without an able son there would have been no founding reign.

sentences.zh: 矧累功積德，未比於周文，創業開基，尚虧於魏祖。

translations.literal: Moreover his piled merit and stored virtue did not equal King Wen of Zhou, and in founding a realm and opening a line he still fell short of Wei's founder.
translations.idiomatic: His piled merit never matched King Wen, and his founding fell short of Cao Cao.

sentences.zh: 追諡為「武」，斯亦幸焉！

translations.literal: To be posthumously styled "Martial" was also a piece of fortune.
translations.idiomatic: That he was posthumously styled "Martial" was itself a mercy.
